Before the Next Big Snow: A Winter Checklist for Your Solar, Battery and Generator

Last January buried the Wabash Valley. Here's how to make sure your backup power is ready for the next one.

Duke Electra

Remember the last weekend of January? The National Weather Service in Indianapolis recorded 9.1 inches at Indianapolis on January 25, 2026, the city's biggest one-day snowfall since 2018, and observers in Vigo County reported 8 to 10.5 inches. The Tribune-Star reported that Vigo County issued local emergency declarations and travel warnings, and the Weather Service followed the snow with an extreme cold warning for wind chills that could reach 20 to 25 below.

It's October now. The next big one is out there somewhere. Accutek Solar has been pulling wire across west-central Indiana and east-central Illinois for 32 years, since 1994, and here's what we'd tell a neighbor: right now, while it's still sweater weather, is the easy time to get your backup power ready. The night the lines come down is not.

"Will My Solar Keep My Power On in an Outage?"

That's the question Accutek Solar hears most. Straight answer: solar panels alone, no. Solar with battery storage, yes.

The U.S. Department of Energy (page checked Oct. 4, 2026) explains that solar systems are designed to switch off when grid power cuts out, for safety reasons, and that solar with a properly configured inverter and battery storage can detect the outage and switch to "islanded" mode to keep the power on. A Clean Energy Group guide (March 2015) spells out the safety part: a system that kept feeding the grid could send power back onto lines crews are repairing, and the UL 1741 inverter standard requires grid-connected inverters to turn off shortly after an outage is detected.

That shutoff protects the lineman working your road. The battery keeps your house running while he works. If you already have storage, know which circuits are on your backed-up panel. If you don't, that's the piece that turns your array into backup power, and Seth and the crew can walk you through it.

Battery Gear: Know Your LiFePO4 Specs

Accutek Solar installs lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) storage, and every battery publishes a spec sheet. Here's what to read on yours, using two EG4 models as examples only, not a recommendation (specs checked Oct. 4, 2026):

  • Capacity and usable capacity. The EG4 LifePower4 48V V2 rack battery is rated 5.12 kWh. The EG4 WallMount All Weather is rated 14.3 kWh. For both, EG4 recommends a state-of-charge floor no lower than 20% to keep to an 80% depth of discharge, so plan on using about 80% of the nameplate.
  • Cycle life. EG4 lists more than 6,000 cycles at 80% depth of discharge for the LifePower4 V2, and more than 8,000 cycles at 0.5C and 80% depth of discharge for the WallMount All Weather.
  • Charging and discharging range. Both list charging from 32°F to about 122°F and discharging from -4°F to about 131°F. In other words, they can deliver power below freezing but only charge above it.
  • Built-in protection. The battery management system on the LifePower4 V2 cuts off charging below 23°F as a safeguard.
  • Self-heating. The WallMount All Weather has a built-in 224-watt heater that turns on when the battery's internal temperature hits 32°F and off at 41°F.
  • Indoor vs. outdoor. The LifePower4 V2 is rated IP20. The WallMount All Weather is rated IP65, and EG4 describes it for residential outdoor energy storage.

Where your battery can go (garage, basement or outside wall) comes down to its manual and local code. Getting that right is part of the install.

Your Generator: Exercise, Service, Cold Weather Kit

A standby generator that sits all year still needs attention. Kohler's operation manual for its 14/20RESA and 20RESC home generators says to run the generator without load once a week for 20 minutes, and that exercising it weekly or every two weeks is required to keep the engine and alternator in good condition. The controller can do it on a schedule. Kohler's maintenance guidance (as of Oct. 4, 2026) says most standby generators should get professional service at least once a year, even if they never ran during an outage. A typical visit covers oil and filter, air filter, spark plug inspection, battery testing and a load test.

Kohler also recommends its Cold Weather Kit for generators installed where the temperature regularly falls below 32°F. As of Oct. 4, 2026, the kit is offered for 14- to 20-kW air-cooled units and includes breather tube, oil and fuel regulator heaters. Kohler's battery heater kit wraps the starting battery and runs on a thermostat that turns the heater on below 60°F and off at 80°F. Not sure what your unit has? Ask before the first hard freeze.

Running a portable generator? The CDC is blunt: never use one inside your home or garage, even with the doors and windows open. Run it outside, more than 20 feet from your home, doors and windows, and install battery-operated or battery back-up carbon monoxide detectors near every sleeping area.

Snow on the Panels: Hands Off the Glass

Panels are built for this. LONGi's module cleaning instructions say its modules are designed to withstand high snow pressure. If you do want to clear them, the same instructions say to brush the snow off gently, not to try to remove frozen ice from the panel surface, and not to use hard or sharp tools that could scratch or crack the tempered glass. Stay off the roof. This is one more place a ground mount earns its keep: it can put the array where you can reach it from the ground with a soft brush.

Your October Checklist

  • Confirm which circuits your battery backs up.
  • Pull up your battery's spec sheet and check where it's installed against its ratings.
  • Make sure your generator's weekly or every-other-week exercise is actually running.
  • Book annual generator service if it's been more than a year, and ask about a cold weather kit.
  • Test the CO detectors near every sleeping area.
  • Build the basic kit. The Indiana Department of Homeland Security recommends water, non-perishable food, flashlights, batteries, a radio and first-aid supplies, plus a plan for medical needs like powered devices and refrigerated medicine.
  • Buy a soft snow brush. Leave the shovel in the garage.
